# Step 1: How I understand the task

## The task in my own words

You're building a forecaster. At some moment **t**, we stand at "now" and ask two questions about a chosen region:

1. **Will there be an air-raid alert in the next H hours?** For example, a probability for each of the next 1, 3 and 6 hours.
2. **If an alert starts, or is already running, how long will it last?**

The rules:
- **No leakage.** At time t the model only knows things that happened before t. That covers alerts that had started, alerts that had ended, and texts that were published. Training and testing follow time order: train on the past and test on the most recent weeks. We never shuffle randomly.
- **Recent data.** We test on the latest period we can actually get, so we have to check how fresh each data source really is.
- **The process matters as much as the score.** We start with simple baselines and improve step by step. Every claim needs output we've actually seen.

## What can realistically be predicted

**Can be predicted, with real signal (I expect this, but haven't verified it on data yet):**
- **Time-of-day and day-of-week patterns.** Drone and missile attacks have tended to cluster at night.
- **Recent activity.** How many alerts there were in the last 24 hours or 7 days, and how long ago the last one ended.
- **Spread between regions.** An alert in a neighboring or frontline region before t raises the chance of one in our region soon after.
- **Duration in broad strokes.** Short alerts tend to be ballistic threats and long ones drone waves. The time of day and what's happening in other regions may also help.
- **Text signals.** Monitoring channels post things like "drones launched" or "bombers took off" before alerts. This is probably the strongest leading signal, but it's also the hardest to collect cleanly and timestamp honestly.

**Cannot be predicted:**
- The exact minute of the next attack. That's an adversary's decision, not a physical process.
- Big strategic changes, like a new campaign or a lull. The model can only catch these after they've started showing up in the data.

So the honest framing is a **probabilistic, short-horizon** forecast. The model learns base rates plus reactions to recent events. It doesn't predict attacks.

## Leakage traps I'll watch for

- **Censoring.** At time t, an ongoing alert has no end time yet. Using its real end time would be leakage.
- **Rolling features.** These must use only data strictly before t.
- **Other regions.** Their alerts count only if they started before t.
- **Timezone and daylight saving.** Kyiv time vs UTC.
- **Text data.** Use the original publication time, not the time a post was edited or scraped.
- **Model tuning.** Hyperparameters get tuned on a validation period, not on the test period.

## Data sources to check (I haven't verified any of these yet)

| Source | What I believe it is | Check here |
|---|---|---|
| Vadimkin's dataset | A GitHub repo with CSVs of official alerts (region, start, end), updated periodically | https://github.com/Vadimkin/ukrainian-air-raid-sirens-dataset |
| alerts.in.ua API | Live alerts and some history; requires a free token. I'm not sure how much history it keeps | https://devs.alerts.in.ua |
| Official Telegram channel "Повітряна тривога" | Alert start and end messages with timestamps; access via the Telegram API (Telethon, needs api_id) | https://t.me/air_alert_ua |
| Kaggle datasets | Various, often out of date | Search "ukraine air raid alerts" on kaggle.com |

My knowledge stops in mid-2026, so I don't know how fresh any of these are as of today (2026-10-10). Checking that is our first real step.

## Decisions for you

**A. Region scope**
- **One region (e.g. Kyiv city):** simplest and easy to explain. Less data, and it ignores spread from other regions as a target.
- **All oblasts, one model:** more data, and it can use neighbors' alerts as inputs. The pipeline is more complex.
- **Middle option:** forecast one or a few target regions, and use all regions' past alerts as inputs.

**B. Forecast setup**
- **Hourly grid (my suggestion):** every hour, predict whether an alert starts in the next H hours. It's simple, easy to evaluate (Brier score, log-loss, calibration) and naturally free of leakage.
- **Time until the next alert (survival model):** more elegant, but harder to evaluate and to explain.

**C. Duration target**
- Duration of an alert at the moment it starts. We only know that it started, not when it ends.
- Remaining duration of an ongoing alert, given how long it has already lasted.
- Both.

**D. Text data**
- **Skip for now:** finish a solid model on alert history first, then add text as a separate experiment that has to beat that model.
- **Include from the start:** more ambitious, but Telegram access and timestamps could eat up time.

Baselines we'll compare against:
- **Seasonal frequency:** the historical rate for each hour of the week.
- **Persistence:** the recent rate continues.
- **Duration:** the median of past durations.

## My questions

1. Did the organizers say anything about region, horizon or deadline?
2. Can you get a Telegram api_id or an alerts.in.ua token, or should we use public files only?
3. Which Python setup do you use (pandas, scikit-learn, LightGBM all fine)?

Once you've decided A–D, the next step is a small script that downloads one candidate dataset and prints its shape, columns and date range. I'll write it only after you approve.

**Assistant:**

Thanks. Here's how I'd handle B and C, and an explanation of D.

## B. Forecast setup: both views from one model

The hourly view and "when is the next alert" don't need two separate models. One model can produce both:
- For each hour ahead (+1h, +2h, … +24h), it gives the probability that an alert starts in that hour, given there was none before it.
- **Hourly view:** a chart of those probabilities.
- **Next alert:** chain the hours together into "the chance the next alert has started by hour k". The predicted time is where that crosses 50%, and we can also show a range (e.g. "most likely between 1:00 and 4:00").

Pros: the two views can never contradict each other, and there's only one model to train and evaluate. Con: it's a bit more complex than a plain yes/no classifier.

**One more decision for B:** how far ahead should we forecast? My suggestion is 24 hours. Shorter horizons are more reliable, and beyond a day it's mostly base rates.

## C. Duration: both

The same trick works here. One duration model gets "minutes already elapsed" as an input:
- elapsed = 0 gives the duration of a new alert;
- elapsed = 40 min gives "the alert has run 40 minutes, how much longer?"

## D. Text data, explained

So far the model learns only from **alert history**: when and where alerts happened, and how long they lasted.

The question was whether to also feed it **text**: news, official statements, or Telegram channels. Here's an example of why that could help. A monitoring channel posts at 21:10 "group of drones heading toward Poltava oblast", and the alert in Poltava starts at 21:25. A model that reads such messages could raise the probability before the alert begins. Alert history alone can't see that.

The leakage rule applies: the model may only use messages published **before** the forecast time.

Difficulties:
- Getting the history needs Telegram API access (your own account and an api_id) or scraping.
- We need archives that cover the whole training period.
- The texts are in Ukrainian, and we'd have to turn them into features.
- It takes significant extra effort.
- I haven't verified which channels have usable archives.

Options:

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **1. No text** | Simplest, focuses on the core | Misses the strongest potential leading signal |
| **2. Text later, as an experiment** (my suggestion) | We first build a working model, then test "with text vs without" on the same period, which is a clear and honest comparison | Might not fit if time runs out |
| **3. Text from the start** | Maximum potential accuracy | High risk of getting stuck on data collection before having any working model |

- **B horizon:** 24 hours OK?
- From my last message: deadline, and what a region should show on the map.

"Text" means messages written by people, as opposed to the alert records themselves.

**Without text**, the model only sees records like:

| region | start | end |
|---|---|---|
| Poltava oblast | 21:25 | 22:40 |

From these it learns patterns: what time of day alerts usually happen, how often, how long they last, and which regions are often alerted together.

**With text**, the model also reads things people wrote before an alert, for example:
- a Telegram channel post: *"21:10 — group of drones heading toward Poltava oblast"*;
- a news article: *"Air Force: missile carriers took off"*.

These messages often appear **before** the alert starts, so they can warn the model early. Records alone can't do that.

**Why it's optional and harder:**
- We'd need to collect thousands of old messages.
- We'd have to teach the program to understand them.
- We must be careful to use only messages written before the forecast moment.

So the question is: should the model use only alert records, or also these messages?

My suggestion is option 2. First we build the model on alert records only. Later, if there's time, we add messages as an experiment and check whether the forecast gets better.

**Assistant:**

Here's how I understand the interface you want:

- **A big map of Ukraine** by region.
- **A time slider** with the forecast hour: now, +1h, +2h, … +24h. Moving it recolors the map.
- **Red** = alert, **gray** = no alert.
- **Region view:** click a region and see how its status is expected to change hour by hour over the next 24 hours, like a timeline strip.

From this I take it the horizon is confirmed as **24 hours**.

There are two important design points.

## 1. Red/gray is a yes/no, but the model gives a probability

The model will say something like "Kharkiv, +5h: 63% chance of alert". To paint red or gray, we need a rule.

| Option | How it looks | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **a. Threshold** | Red if probability > X% (e.g. 50%), else gray | Exactly what you described, very clear | Hides uncertainty: 51% and 99% look the same |
| **b. Gradient** | From gray to red, the stronger the red, the higher the probability | Honest, shows confidence | Not a strict red/gray |
| **c. Threshold + numbers** | Red/gray like (a), with the exact % on hover or click and in the region panel | Clear map, and the detail is still available | Slightly more work |

My suggestion is **c**. The threshold itself shouldn't be guessed: we'd choose it on the validation period, the one that gives the most correct red/gray calls.

## 2. "Red at +5h" means an active alert, which is a different question

So far we planned to predict **when an alert starts** (D5) and **how long it lasts** (D6). The map needs something else: **"is an alert active in this region at hour +5?"** An alert that started at +3h and lasts 3 hours makes +5h red.

| Option | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **a. Separate model for "active at +h"** | Trained directly on "was there an active alert h hours later?" | Directly matches the map, easy to test honestly | A third model, and it can slightly disagree with the panel |
| **b. Combine start + duration models** | Simulate many possible futures from D5 + D6 and count how often the region is red at each hour | All views come from one consistent logic | More complex, and errors in the two models add up |

My suggestion is **a** for the map, keeping D5/D6 for the "next alert" and "duration" info in the region panel. It's simpler and directly testable, and we can check the disagreement between them as a sanity test.

## Region view (24h)

For the selected region:
- **Top:** a 24-cell strip, one cell per hour, colored red or gray.
- **Below:** the probability curve for each hour.
- **Plus:** "next alert most likely around HH:MM" and the expected duration, or the remaining duration if an alert is active now.

Yes, I understand, and you're right: my plan didn't show it. I described the project as an engineering pipeline (data, features, models, map). The "features" I listed were ad hoc ideas, and the map took a large part of the plan. There was no mathematical model of the process itself. That's a mistake, and I'll record it in NOTES.md as M2.

Here's how to make mathematics the foundation of every part.

## 1. Describe alerts as a mathematical process

For each region r, the alert status over time is an **on/off process**: X_r(t) = 1 during an alert and 0 otherwise. The process has two parts.

**a) When alerts start: a point process with an intensity function.**

λ_r(t | history before t) is the instantaneous rate at which an alert starts in region r. Every forecast follows from it. A natural form is a **multivariate Hawkes process**, a model where events make further events more likely:

λ_r(t) = μ_r(t) + Σ_s Σ_{alerts i in region s before t} α_rs · g(t − t_i)

- **μ_r(t)**, the baseline rate: daily and weekly cycles, modeled with Fourier terms (sine/cosine).
- **α_rr**, self-excitation: an alert in a region makes another one soon more likely.
- **α_rs**, cross-excitation: an alert in region s raises the rate in region r, which captures attack waves moving across the country.
- **g**, a decay kernel, e.g. exponential: the influence fades with time.
- While an alert is active, a new start in the same region is impossible. The intensity only applies in the "off" state.

This turns our hypotheses into **parameters with confidence intervals**:
- H1 (night clustering) is the shape of μ_r(t).
- H3 (neighbors' influence) is whether α_rs > 0.
- H4 (recent activity matters) is whether α_rr > 0.

They get confirmed or rejected by numbers, not by my words.

**b) How long alerts last: survival analysis.**

The duration D is modeled by its survival function S(d) = P(D > d), with censoring handled correctly: alerts still active at the cut-off time are not thrown away.
- Candidate distributions: log-normal, Weibull, or a **mixture**. If durations form two groups (short and long), a two-component mixture fits better. That's a mathematical test of H2.
- **Remaining duration** after e minutes follows from an exact formula: P(D > e + x | D > e) = S(e + x) / S(e). This answers both duration questions with one model, which is the math behind D6.

## 2. All map outputs come from one model

Once λ and S are fitted, the model is a **generative** one: it can simulate the future. From the state at time t:
1. Simulate thousands of possible next-24-hour scenarios (Monte Carlo).
2. **P(alert active at +h)** is the share of scenarios where X_r(t+h) = 1. This is the map color.
3. **The time to the next alert** comes from the same scenarios.
4. **Duration** comes from S.

All three outputs are mathematically consistent. This answers Q10: option b, now with a solid foundation. The map is just a picture of P(X_r(t+h) = 1 | history).

## 3. Time-series analysis before modeling

Each step produces numbers that justify the model's structure:
- **Rates by hour of the week** show whether a cycle exists and its shape.
- **Distribution of gaps between alerts:** if alerts were random (Poisson), the gaps would be exponential. Clustering shows up as overdispersion, a variance-to-mean ratio above 1, and that justifies the Hawkes model.
- **Autocorrelation and cross-correlation** of hourly counts between regions show the lead-lag structure, i.e. who gets alerted first.
- **Change-point detection** finds when the process changed, which tells us how much history to train on.
- **Duration fits** with QQ plots and likelihood comparison choose the distribution.

## 4. A ladder of models

Each level must beat the previous one on the same test windows, by a proper score:

| Level | Model | Tests which hypothesis |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | Inhomogeneous Poisson (seasonal rate only) | baseline: "nights are dangerous" |
| M1 | + self-excitation | H4 |
| M2 | + cross-region excitation | H3 |
| M3 | + regime adaptation (training window or weighting) | non-stationarity |
| M4 | + text as an external input to λ | H5 |
| ML | Gradient boosting on the same inputs, as a challenger | Is flexibility worth losing interpretability? |

M0 is exactly the "model just learned nights" case. If M1/M2 don't beat it, we report that honestly.

## 5. Mathematical evaluation

- **Proper scoring rules:** log-likelihood and Brier score on future windows, with walk-forward testing.
- **Goodness of fit with the time-rescaling theorem:** if the model is correct, the transformed gaps between alerts must follow an exponential distribution with mean 1. We check this with a KS test. It's a standard and strict check for point-process models.
- **Calibration:** when the model says 30%, does an alert happen about 30% of the time?
- **Significance:** are improvements between levels larger than the noise across test windows?
- **Duration:** log-score and CRPS, accounting for censoring.

## Honest caveats

- These are **candidate** models. The data may show something else, and then we follow the data, not the plan.
- I'm not sure a ready-made Hawkes library works on your Python and Mac. We can implement the likelihood ourselves with scipy, which is fully transparent. A simpler alternative is an hourly logistic model whose inputs are exactly the Hawkes kernel sums; mathematically it's a discretized version of the same process.

## Your decision

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Math model only** (point process + survival) | Fully interpretable, every number has meaning | May miss complex patterns |
| **B. Machine learning only** (gradient boosting) | Flexible | A black box, hypotheses aren't tested as parameters |
| **C. Math model as the core, ML as a challenger** (my suggestion) | Interpretable core, plus an honest check of whether ML adds anything | More work |

I found several GitHub projects that forecast Ukrainian air raid alerts with machine learning. They vary in approach, and most are research or student projects rather than production warning tools.

- **Nujabesuuu/AlarmForecast** is a full-stack app that gives hour-by-hour alert probabilities for all 25 regions, 24 hours ahead. Its pipeline pulls alert history, weather, Telegram channels, and ISW war reports into a LightGBM model behind a Flask API and a Next.js map. The repo reports ROC-AUC 0.91 and F1 0.73 on held-out data.
- **lbgos/AirAlerts** forecasts the chance of a siren starting in each oblast within 30 minutes, 1 hour, 3 hours, or 6 hours. It uses per-horizon LightGBM models with Platt calibration, and it includes a live mode that polls a Telegram alert channel.
- **Dopplerr24/air-raid-alert-analysis** estimates, for each region and hour, the probability that a new alert starts within the next hour. It uses a single shared LightGBM classifier and a leakage-free validation setup, and it reports PR-AUC and Brier-skill results.
- **koalla05/air-alerts** predicts how much longer an active alert will last and how long quiet periods between alerts will run. It is framed as a statistical experiment and research benchmark.
- **maranferij-lang/Ukraine-air-alerts** asks whether an alert will occur in each oblast within the next 1, 3, or 6 hours, using one model with oblast as a feature. It compares against baselines.
- **Ddrakkx/alerts-forecast** gives probabilistic forecasts of alert onsets in Poltava oblast, using the public Ukrainian air raid sirens dataset.
- **3olena3/air-raid-alerts-forecast** and **mykoladomanskyi25-dotcom/Air-raid-alerts** are time-series analyses. The second compares simple baselines, such as naive persistence and rolling means, on oblast-level daily counts.

Several projects state clearly that they are not warning systems. The koalla05 repo says it must never replace official alerts from Ukraine's State Emergency Service or official siren channels, and the Dopplerr24 repo says the same. Treat these as research or learning projects, and rely on official channels for safety.

The main arXiv study I found is **"Predictive Analytics of Air Alerts in the Russian-Ukrainian War"** (arXiv:2411.14625), by Demian Pavlyshenko and Bohdan Pavlyshenko. It was submitted in November 2024 under cs.LG, cs.AI, and cs.CY. The paper considers exploratory data analysis and approaches in predictive analytics for air alerts during the Russian-Ukrainian war.

**Key findings:**
- Alerts in neighboring regions are informative. The alert status in a particular region is highly dependable on the features of its adjacent regions.
- Calendar effects matter. Seasonality features like hours, days of a week and months are also crucial in predicting the target variable.
- The authors used a 1-minute granularity time series. They created an alert_ts dataframe with the time series index from Mar 25 2022 to Nov 6 2024 with the granularity of 1 minute.

**A scope inconsistency:** The abstract describes predicting alerts expected in a region within a set period, but the introduction says the main goal is to conduct an exploratory data analysis and create a predictive model to forecast the duration of air alerts. I only saw snippets, so check the full PDF to see which target the models actually use.

**Newer, non-arXiv work:** Several GitHub projects take a similar approach and are more recent. I haven't verified their results beyond the snippets shown, and they aren't peer-reviewed:
- **lbgos/AirAlerts** forecasts the probability that a siren starts in an oblast within 30 minutes to 6 hours. It reports calibration and AUC, with a test period of 2026-09-25 to 2026-10-09. Its AUC ranges from 0.86 to 0.92 across horizons.
- **vladysalvkrutii/kse-air-alerts** produces hourly per-oblast probabilities that a new alert starts within 3 hours, and it is built to avoid using information from after its forecast time.
- **Dopplerr24/air-raid-alert-analysis** uses a national panel model covering 24 regions with one shared LightGBM classifier.
- **mykoladomanskyi25-dotcom/Air-raid-alerts** is a baseline study. Its best model was a 7-day rolling mean, which wins not by finding signal but by smoothing noise, and it misses mass-strike spikes.

The searches didn't surface a peer-reviewed venue version of the arXiv paper, so I can't confirm whether it was published elsewhere.

I didn't find a paper that applies a Hawkes process to Ukrainian air raid alerts. The results include related work on each part of the query, though.

**Closest match on the alert data:** A working paper from the University of Chicago Becker Friedman Institute studies Ukraine's government alert system after the February 2022 invasion. It uses the Air Alert app's alert records and device movement data to test whether people respond when alerts go out. Public response to government alerts saves lives in Ukraine following the February 2022 invasion by Russian forces. Its method is a quasi-experimental design, not a point process model. It does use alert timing and region-level counts, which could serve as inputs to a Hawkes model. The paper is marked as a draft, so check the latest version. This quasi-experimental approach provides credible estimates of the response effects.

**Hawkes process applied to Ukrainian conflict events:** A 2024 arXiv paper models the 2013–2014 Euromaidan protests with a discretized Hawkes process. The authors chose it because the nature of our dataset, presenting a daily sum of events, necessitates the use of a discretized variation. This is the most similar methodological precedent for daily Ukrainian event counts.

**Hawkes process background:** Several sources explain the model:
- Each event excites the process, heightening the probability of upcoming events. For alerts, this would mean one alert raises the short-term chance of another.
- The branching ratio (ρ) must be within the range (0, 1) for the process to remain stationary. This is a key check when fitting a Hawkes model to alert data.
- On the small subset, the Hawkes model exhibited the highest log-likelihood, indicating that short-term excitation is detectable at fine time scales. This comes from a cybersecurity paper, but it shows the fine-versus-coarse time-scale issue that would matter for alert data.

**Other context:** Alerts are triggered by radar tracking. Regions that lie on the path of the detected threat are notified, which suggests that alerts may cluster in time and space, a pattern a spatio-temporal Hawkes model could capture. A review of spatio-temporal Hawkes models is available in the *Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Environmental Statistics* (2025).

If you're after a specific paper, I'd suggest searching Google Scholar or arXiv for "Hawkes" with "air alert" or "sirens" and "Ukraine," or checking the Air Alert app's data sources in any academic work you find.

**Найближче за темою:**
- Дипломна робота з Харківського університету радіоелектроніки описує ML-модель прогнозування стихійних лих. Здійснено прогнозування стихійних лих на основі сучасних методів машинного навчання із реальних кліматичних даних, з використанням AutoML (H2O) та LSTM. Це схожа постановка задачі: часові ряди, класифікація подій рідкісного класу і пояснення результатів через SHAP. Для тривог це релевантно, бо тривоги теж рідкісні події.
- Пошук також показав прогноз загроз від новини про масований удар. Він не є моделлю тривог: це оцінка ймовірних дат і цілей, яку, за повідомленням, зробили штучний інтелект і три моделі. У висновку усі три моделі вважають, що найближчими днями зберігатиметься загроза нового масованого удару. Методологія там не розкрита, тому довіряти їй як науковому результату не варто.

- **Model:** LightGBM. The page says it was chosen over logistic regression, linear regression, decision tree, LinearSVC and XGBoost baselines. The author's own baselines were linear regression (F1 0.67) and a tuned decision tree (F1 0.68, ROC-AUC 0.80).
- **Evaluation:** The page says "time-series cross-validation" and "region-aware time-series cross-validation." Reported LightGBM test metrics:

  - PR-AUC 0.831 ± 0.025

- **Test period:** Not stated explicitly. The only dates given are the Telegram data range (Feb 2022 to Mar 2026) and the live snapshot.
- **Leakage:** Not explicitly addressed. Time-series CV is mentioned, but the page does not describe how leakage is prevented.
- **Recency:** The live demo shows a forecast made on 15 April 2026 at 19:20, covering the following 24 hours. The system recomputes hourly and retrains weekly. The footer shows © 2026, but no explicit last-update date appears.

**Tool result:**

```
**Ukraine Air Raid Alerts: Real-Time Duration & Expiration Predictor** is a public GitHub repository (koalla05/air-alerts) with four commits and no stated license. The README describes it as a statistical and machine learning system for predicting remaining alert durations and quiet times between alerts across Ukrainian oblasts.

- **Predictions:**
  - **Task A (active alert):** the probability that an alert ends within a given window, plus the median remaining time and an uncertainty range. Windows are 15, 30, and 60 minutes.
  - **Task B (quiet period):** the probability that the next alert starts within a given window, plus the expected gap. Windows are 1, 3, and 6 hours.
- **Framing:** The README treats this as a time-to-event (survival analysis) problem, conditioning on elapsed time.
- **Methods:**
  - Empirical conditional quantile baseline
  - Kaplan-Meier survival baseline
  - LightGBM quantile regressors at the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles
  - LightGBM binary classifiers for the event windows above
- **Data:** The Vadimkin Ukrainian Air Raid Sirens Dataset, with more than 299,000 records from March 2022 to September 2026. After cleaning, it contains 65,172 episodes across 24 oblasts. Sub-minute glitches and extreme outliers were removed.
- **Evaluation:** Pinball loss, coverage, MAE, Brier score, and ROC-AUC, per the project structure. The README reports sample outputs, such as a 30-minute active alert in Kyiv City, but gives no aggregate results.
- **Leakage handling:** A chronological, point-in-time split trains on older data and tests on held-out recent months, to prevent future data from leaking into training.
- **Test period:** Only "held-out recent months" is stated, with no specific dates.
- **Interface:** A Python pipeline class, a CLI training script, and a Jupyter notebook. No map or web UI is mentioned.
- **KSE:** The page does not mention KSE.
- **Disclaimer:** The README states the project is a statistical experiment and research benchmark, not a civil defense tool, and must not replace official alerts from Ukraine's State Emergency Service.

**Tool result:**

```
**Target and horizons:** The project forecasts, for each Ukrainian oblast, the probability of a siren start (oblasts not under alert) or an all-clear (oblasts under alert). Horizons are 15 minutes, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 3 hours, and 6 hours. Forecasts are described as calibrated, meaning "a forecast of 70% should come true about 70% of the time."

**Duration prediction:** Yes, in part. The all-clear model estimates the probability that an alert ends within each horizon, and its features include how long the current alert has run.

**Data sources:**
- @UkraineAlarmSignal (Telegram): alert starts and ends, and threat notes, tagged by oblast. This is the label source and the main feature source.
- @kpszsu and @deraketaua (radar channels): posts about drones and missiles, converted to structured events by a local TF-IDF plus logistic regression classifier. The final model does not use them.
- Data was scraped with Telethon for 2025-12-01 onward. The page's date range reads "2025-12-01 to 2026-10-09." Older 2022–2024 data was excluded.

**Model:** LightGBM, one model per horizon, with recent days weighted more heavily (60-day half-life). Calibration uses Platt scaling on the last 7 days, followed by a conservative binning cap that limits how certain a forecast can be.

**Features:** Time of day, the oblast's own recent alerts and threats, neighboring oblasts, second-ring neighbors, national counts, and last-minute activity. All features use only events before time T.

**Evaluation:**
- Metrics: Brier score, AUC, expected calibration error (ECE), the share of confident (≤20% or ≥80%) forecasts that were wrong, a log-loss penalty, and a "points" score relative to climatology.
- Validation: a time-based split into train, calibrate, and test sets, with a separate 14-day dev window for model selection. The final test window was the last 14 days, ending 2026-10-10 16:20 UTC.

**Reported final-test results (siren starts, model f1s_recent_cons):**
- 15m: Brier 0.058 (climatology 0.069), AUC 0.89, ECE 0.018
- 30m: Brier 0.090 (climatology 0.114), AUC 0.88, ECE 0.024
- 1h: Brier 0.118 (climatology 0.164), AUC 0.88, ECE 0.025
- 3h: Brier 0.127 (climatology 0.207), AUC 0.90, ECE 0.030
- 6h: Brier 0.112 (climatology 0.200), AUC 0.92, ECE 0.037

All-clear results (model f1c_recent_cons) are also reported per horizon, with AUCs from 0.77 (15m) to 0.88 (6h).

**Leakage handling:** Features use only information before T. Train, calibration, and test sets are separated in time and "purged so no label window crosses a boundary." The alert-duration rule uses a 24-hour expiry for lost posts, and the README notes this was changed from an earlier 3-hour expiry.

**Map and UI:** Live mode polls the alert channel every 30 seconds and serves a one-page UI in Ukrainian and English, with dark and light themes, a horizon dropdown, and a map shaded red for siren-start probability and blue for all-clear probability. Map geometry comes from geoBoundaries (OpenStreetMap, ODbL). Live forecasts are logged and can be scored with `forecast score-live`.

**KSE:** The page does not mention KSE.
```

**Tool result:**

```
**Repository:** vladysalvkrutii/kse-air-alerts, a KSE Stage 2 project forecasting Ukrainian air raid alerts.

- **Prediction target:** For each whole hour (UTC), the probability that a new alert starts in a region within the next 3 hours. The page stresses that the target is a start, not an alert that is already active.
- **Regions:** 24 oblasts. Luhansk is excluded because its permanent alert is not in the data, and Crimea is not in the data.
- **Duration prediction:** No. The page does not describe predicting how long an alert lasts.
- **Text data:** No. Text, Telegram, and news features are listed under "Not used."
- **Map/UI:** None described. Outputs are written to a `results/` folder by a command-line script (`run.py`).

**Data sources**
- Vadimkin/ukrainian-air-raid-sirens-dataset, specifically the eTryvoga volunteer file, pinned to a specific commit.
- 115,790 alerts from 2022-02-25 to 2026-10-09. The last 24 hours are dropped.
- The official data in the same repo was rejected because it ends on 2026-09-07.
- About 10% of alerts are marked "naive" (no end message).

**Model**
- Logistic regression (scikit-learn) with standardized features and region one-hot encoding.
- Trained on the last 16 weeks, chosen on validation from 8, 16, 26, and 40 weeks.
- Features include recent alert start counts, time since the last start, whether an alert is running, and Kyiv hour of day.

**Baselines:** base rate, hour-of-day climatology, day-of-week × hour climatology, persistence (raw and calibrated), and seasonal naive (24 h and 168 h).

**Evaluation**
- Walk-forward validation with weekly refits: 14 Aug – 11 Sep 2026 (4 folds), used for all design choices.
- Final test: 11 Sep – 9 Oct 2026 (4 folds), 16,080 region-hours, 48.6% positive.
- Metrics: Brier score, within-region AUC, and a calibration table.

**Test results (Brier / within-region AUC / skill vs. climatology)**
- Logistic regression (16 weeks): 0.1762 / 0.570 / +7.4%
- Calibrated persistence: 0.1892 / 0.492 / +0.5%
- Climatology (hour-of-day): 0.1902 / 0.546 / 0
- Base rate: 0.1909 / 0.486 / −0.4%
- Climatology (day-of-week × hour): 0.1964 / 0.542 / −3.2%
- Seasonal naive 24 h: 0.3312 / 0.527 / −74%
- Seasonal naive 168 h: 0.3430 / 0.510 / −80%
- Persistence (raw 0/1): 0.3515 / 0.502 / −85%

The model has the best Brier score in each of the four test weeks. On validation, its Brier score was 0.1571 versus 0.1663 for the best baseline.

**Calibration:** Accurate above about 40%. It under-predicts in the 10–30% range.

**Leakage handling**
- A test file (`tests/test_no_leakage.py`) checks that features computed from full data, from only what an observer knew at time t, and from data with fake future alerts are identical.
- Alerts marked "naive" are treated as running until the next start in that region.
- The test includes two deliberately leaky features that must make it fail.
- Training examples are used only if their label window closed before each fold starts.

**Limitations stated by the author:** The gain over the best baseline is modest. Within-region ranking is weak. The model lags rising alert frequency. Only one label source is used, and it disagrees with official data in some regions. The test window is short, so small baseline differences may be noise.

```
**Repository:** Dopplerr24/air-raid-alert-analysis (GitHub, public)

- **Prediction target:** Whether a new air raid alert starts within the next hour. The README describes it as the probability that "a new air raid alert starts within the next hour" for each region and hour. The target is onset, not whether an alert is active, to avoid rewarding persistence.
- **Unit and spatial grain:** One row per (hour, region), at oblast level. Raion and hromada alerts roll up to their oblast.
- **Regions:** A national panel of 24 regions. Luhanska oblast is excluded and Crimea is absent. An earlier single-region study covered Kyiv City.
- **Data source:** The official file from Vadimkin/ukrainian-air-raid-sirens-dataset, with times in UTC. The volunteer file was not used.
- **Model type:** One global LightGBM binary classifier with fixed hyperparameters (depth 6, 31 leaves, 400 trees, learning rate 0.05). Baselines include base rates, persistence, and hour-of-week climatology.
- **Evaluation:** Walk-forward validation with 5 folds of 90 days each, covering 14 Jun 2025 to 7 Sep 2026, and a 24-hour embargo between train and test. The dataset has 938,592 region-hours with an 8.3% positive rate.
- **Reported metrics (fold means):**
  - Primary model (LightGBM global, default): PR-AUC pooled "0.324", PR-AUC macro "0.248", Brier "0.0699", Brier skill "0.116".
  - With `--adjacency`: pooled "0.337", macro "0.263", Brier "0.0691", Brier skill "0.126".
  - Region base rate baseline: pooled "0.152".
  - ROC-AUC is deliberately not reported.
- **Leakage handling:** Features use only past values through a shift function that rejects non-positive lags. Rolling windows are computed after shifting, and alert intervals are clipped. Regions are processed separately to prevent bleed between them. Two tests (causality and region isolation) run before training and abort the run on failure. Base rates, climatology, and tree fitting all happen inside each training fold.
- **Duration prediction:** No. The model predicts onset timing. The EDA script includes a duration chart, but that is exploratory only.
- **Text data:** No text data is mentioned. The inputs are alert time intervals and derived hourly features.
- **Map/UI:** No map or interactive interface is described. `eda_visuals.py` writes three static charts (timing, duration, threat migration) to a `figures/` folder.
- **KSE:** Not mentioned.

I didn't find a peer-reviewed 2025 journal article on air alert duration in Ukraine. The closest matches are an analytics piece, a preprint, and live tracking sites.

- **Lost-lessons analysis (VoxUkraine, April 2025):** This is the most relevant 2025 piece. Using alert data from September 2024 to February 2025, it reports a median alert length of 33 minutes for weekday daytime alerts. The median duration of an air raid alert in Ukraine announced on weekdays between 8:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. from September 2024 to February 2025 was 33 minutes. This means that in most cases, alerts did not last the full 45 minutes of a typical lesson in grades 5–9. The authors draw their alert data from an open GitHub dataset that is sourced and updated from official channels via eAlert. It is an analytics article, not a peer-reviewed study.

- **Predictive analytics preprint (arXiv, November 2024):** Pavlyshenko and Pavlyshenko analyze minute-level alert data from March 2022 to November 2024. The main goal of our study is to conduct an exploratory data analysis and create a predictive model to forecast the duration of air alerts. It is a preprint from late 2024, so it doesn't meet your 2025 date, and I couldn't confirm whether it was later published in a journal. A third-party review summarizes its finding that air alerts in a Ukrainian region can be predicted 5 to 15 minutes ahead from neighbor regions' alert status and the calendar.

I found a repository that matches your description closely, plus a few related ones.

**Best match: vladysalvkrutii/kse-air-alerts.** Its README labels the project as a KSE Stage 2 entry. It forecasts, for each hour and each of 24 regions, the probability that a new alert begins within the next three hours. Forecasts are scored with the Brier score, within-region AUC, and a calibration table. The author deliberately rejected a pooled AUC across regions because it mostly rewards knowing which regions are busier. The data comes from a volunteer-run dataset, and the repo's commit history includes 115,790 alerts from 2022-02-25 through 2026-10-09. The repo also contains a NOTES.md file and a results folder, which may hold more detail.

**Related KSE project: Ddrakkx/alerts-forecast.** This one was built as a mini-project for the KSE Agentic AI School selection. It targets Poltava oblast and predicts alert onsets over 1-, 3-, and 6-hour windows. Its README describes the method as planned, with simple baselines such as recent activity and hour-of-week averages.

**Other KSE-related result:** andriiboichuk13/ua_alerts_analysis is a time series analysis of Ukrainian air raid alerts for KSE Agentic AI School. The README I retrieved had little beyond its description.

**Note on naming:** The vladysalvkrutii repo calls its program the "KSE CS selection," while the other two say "KSE Agentic AI School." If you're looking for a specific submission, check the repo's README or NOTES.md to confirm which program it was built for.

I didn't find any live or stage-specific alert forecast output in the search results. To see current forecasts, you'd need to open the repos directly and run their code.

Команда IT фахівців Stfalcon створила офіційний Telegram Bot додатку “Повітряна тривога” для інформування населення України про загрози артобстрілу й інших небезпек.
- Бот @airalarm_updates_bot, за описом у статті, надсилає сповіщення залежно від вашого місцезнаходження. Також з'явився новий Telegram-бот **@airalarm_updates_bot**, що надсилає індивідуальні повідомлення про тривогу залежно від вашого місцезнаходження.

I found several GitHub projects that forecast Ukrainian air raid alerts, but none of the results mention a Hawkes process. The closest match on survival analysis is koalla05/air-alerts.

- **koalla05/air-alerts** is the best match for "duration" and "survival." It frames predicting how long an alert remains as a conditional time-to-event problem, because users query the system while an alert is already running. It uses LightGBM classifiers for the chance an alert ends within 15, 30, or 60 minutes, and the chance one starts within 1, 3, or 6 hours. It is built on the Vadimkin sirens dataset, and its README says it is a research benchmark, not a civil defense tool. ([github.com/koalla05/air-alerts](https://github.com/koalla05/air-alerts))
- **Dopplerr24/air-raid-alert-analysis** forecasts the probability that a new alert starts in each region within the next hour. It uses walk-forward validation across 24 regions and reports pooled PR-AUC. Its limitations section notes that results cover only one 15-month period and have no confidence intervals. ([github.com/Dopplerr24/air-raid-alert-analysis](https://github.com/Dopplerr24/air-raid-alert-analysis))
- **lbgos/AirAlerts** gives calibrated probabilities that a siren starts in an oblast within 30 minutes, 1, 3, or 6 hours. It uses LightGBM per horizon, weights recent days more heavily, and applies Platt calibration. Its reported AUC ranges from 0.86 to 0.92 on the final test window. ([github.com/lbgos/AirAlerts](https://github.com/lbgos/AirAlerts))
- **vladysalvkrutii/kse-air-alerts** forecasts whether a new alert starts within the next 3 hours for each oblast, using weekly refits in a walk-forward setup. It treats "starts" rather than "is active" as the target, to avoid an alert that is already running winning by default. ([github.com/vladysalvkrutii/kse-air-alerts](https://github.com/vladysalvkrutii/kse-air-alerts))
- **mykoladomanskyi25-dotcom/Air-raid-alerts** is an EDA and baseline project. It compares naive, 7-day rolling mean, and seasonal naive forecasts, and it drops alarms longer than 6 hours as likely stale records. ([github.com/mykoladomanskyi25-dotcom/Air-raid-alerts](https://github.com/mykoladomanskyi25-dotcom/Air-raid-alerts))
- **Nujabesuuu/AlarmForecast** is a full-stack app that forecasts alerts for the next 24 hours, using alert history, weather, Telegram, and ISW reports. ([github.com/Nujabesuuu/AlarmForecast](https://github.com/Nujabesuuu/AlarmForecast))

There is also a published paper on predicting air alert duration. A review of it flags a circularity problem: the own-region duration feature is not lagged and the target includes ongoing alerts, so part of its reported performance is just persistence of the current state. ([pith.science review](https://pith.science/paper/2411.14625))

For a Hawkes or point-process model specifically, you may need a narrower search, such as "self-exciting" or "Hawkes" with "sirens" and "Ukraine."

**Tool result:**

```
**Models and target:** The paper uses random-forest classifiers, one per target region (Lvivska, Vinnytska, Kyivska, and Kharkivska oblasts). Each predicts whether the target region will be under alert within a set horizon. Inputs are cumulative alert-duration features for all regions, plus month, day of week, hour, and a days-since-start counter.

**Horizon:** 5 minutes (main setup) and 15 minutes (second setup).

**Main criticisms (from the AI review):**

- **Leakage/circularity (major):** The target region's own cumulative alert-duration feature is unlagged. For an ongoing alert, it nearly encodes the target, so the model can score well by persistence. The review says the feature-importance rankings therefore don't support the claim that neighboring regions matter most.
- **No baselines or ablation (major):** There is no persistence baseline, no no-skill baseline, no logistic regression comparison, and no ablation removing the target region's own feature.
- **Weak evaluation (major):** A single chronological split at 2024-07-01 is used, with no error bars, repeated runs, or hyperparameter sensitivity analysis.
- **Incomplete specification (major):** The exact final feature set and target construction are not fully described, and the data-preparation code is missing, which hinders reproducibility.
- **Minor issues:** Typos and a duplicated figure title, a missing dataset access date, and no discussion of whether the "ndays" trend is real or an artifact.

The review is machine-generated and has not been checked by a human expert.

I didn't find any source that fits a self-exciting or Hawkes model to Ukrainian air raid siren or alert data. The results contain general Hawkes-process methodology and some background on how the alert systems work.

**Relevant methodology**
- A 2024 arXiv paper on the 2013–2014 Euromaidan protests uses a Hawkes process. It describes the self-exciting property as clustering or bursts of activity, where one event raises the chance of more events nearby (This self-exciting property implies that the occurrence of an event can increase the likelihood of more events happening in its vicinity, forming clusters or bursts of activity.). Its intensity combines a baseline rate with the lingering effect of past events, weighted by a kernel (This intensity function is influenced by both the baseline event rate and the impact of past events.).
- A paper on terror insurgencies gives the general conditional-intensity form, with a baseline term plus a triggering term summed over past events. It also notes that the kernel determines whether excitation is local or longer-lasting in space and time (Depending on the kernel, the excitation may be local or have longer term effects in space and/or time).

**A caveat for alert data**
- A 2026 paper on IDS alert time series found that a Hawkes model fit best on a small subset, but the excitation parameter shrank substantially on the full dataset. The global behavior looked more like a smoothly varying non-homogeneous Poisson process (On the small subset, the Hawkes model exhibited the highest log-likelihood, indicating that short-term excitation is detectable at fine time scales. However, when scaling the analysis to the full dataset, the estimated Hawkes excitation parameter diminished substantially.). Short-term clustering may therefore not hold across an entire conflict period.

**Context on how alerts work**
- Ukraine's system is reportedly moving toward sirens that activate only where there is a missile-attack risk, with alerts sent on a zone-by-zone basis (This will allow for faster transmission of alerts to mobile phone users and activation of air raid sirens only in places where there is a risk of missile attack.).
- Alerts often come in sequences tied to attacks. One NPR report describes an initial siren, followed by a phone-app update after about 15 minutes that is either an all-clear or a warning that the region is targeted (The initial siren often means Ukraine has detected Russian war planes, armed with long-range missiles, taking off hundreds of miles away deep inside Russia. After 15 minutes or so, the phone app usually provides an update.).

**My inference:** Because attacks come in waves and alerts follow one another, a Hawkes model could plausibly fit short-term alert clustering in Ukraine. The IDS result suggests the fit might weaken over longer periods, so a time-varying baseline would likely be needed. This is my own reasoning, not a finding from these sources.

## Short answer

The topic is **not unique**. There are at least 12 similar projects, and at least 3 of them are **other KSE Agentic AI School applications** for the same task. Two are full systems with a 24-hour map, and one already uses Telegram text.

What I did **not** find anywhere is our mathematical core:
- a point-process (Hawkes) model of alert starts with cross-region influence;
- one generative model that gives start, duration and "active at +h" consistently, through simulation;
- the time-rescaling goodness-of-fit test;
- forecasts at hromada level.

Not finding something doesn't prove it doesn't exist, but that's where our project can stand out.

A relevant warning comes from an [IDS alert paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.14299): self-excitation was strong at short time scales but faded over the full dataset. So a Hawkes model needs a time-varying baseline, and that's a risk for our hypothesis H4.

## What this means for us

**1. Honest results are modest.** Projects that measure carefully within each region report small gains over baselines (+7% Brier skill, AUC 0.57–0.69), and one found no gain at all for Poltava. Very high numbers like AUC 0.91 come from pooling all regions together or have unclear test setups. Our model must expect modest gains and report them honestly.

**2. Data freshness is a real problem.** This is a warning, still to be verified by us. Two projects say the **official** file in the Vadimkin dataset **ends 2026-09-07**. One says the volunteer file is unreliable after mid-2025, while another used it up to 2026-10-09. One project reports a feed outage from Aug 29 to Sep 3. lbgos solved freshness by scraping Telegram directly. This makes Step 4 critical.

**3. Lessons worth adopting** (with credit, not copying code):
- an automated leakage test using deliberately leaky features;
- per-region metrics instead of pooled ones;
- exclusion of Luhansk (permanent alert) and Crimea (not in the data).

**4. Text has been tried.** One project found news counts (GDELT) didn't help, and another uses Telegram in its LightGBM model but doesn't show a with-vs-without comparison. Our D7 rule ("keep a source only if it beats without it") is exactly the right test.

## Where we can stand out (your decision)

| Option | What makes it different | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| **a. Mathematical core** (our D10/D11) | Hawkes point process + survival + simulation; hypotheses tested as parameters; time-rescaling goodness-of-fit. Not found in any project | The excitation effect may turn out weak (the IDS warning). Even then we learn something real and can report it |
| b. Hromada-level forecasts | No project forecasts below oblast level | Depends on data existing (Step 4) |
| c. Rigorous text evaluation | Clean with-vs-without comparison of text sources | Telegram access effort |

My suggestion is to keep **a** as the core, which matches what you already chose, and add **b** and **c** only if the data allows.

## Limits of this research

- The search engine is US-based, and I searched in English and Ukrainian. Closed systems, Telegram bots or Ukrainian university theses could still exist.
- The numbers are the authors' claims, taken from their READMEs.
- Some KSE repos are other applicants' work in progress, and they may change.

- **Automated leakage test:** features computed from (1) full data, (2) data cut at time t, and (3) data with fake future alerts added must all be identical. Two deliberately leaky features must make the test fail. For our model: λ(t) computed from cut data must equal λ(t) from full data.
- **They pin the dataset to a specific commit** and drop the last 24h, which may be incomplete. That's good for reproducibility.
- **About 10% of alerts have no end message**, which they treat as running until the next start. That's a censoring issue for our survival model.
- **They chose the training window (8/16/26/40 weeks) on validation, and 16 won.** That's evidence the process changes over time, and it supports M3.
- **Their stated limitation: "the model lags rising alert frequency".** This is exactly what Hawkes self-excitation is designed to fix, a strong motivation for M1.
- Within-region AUC instead of pooled AUC.

- **[IDS Hawkes paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.14299):** excitation looked strong at short scales but faded on the full dataset. This is **the most important mathematical warning for us**: if the baseline μ(t) is too rigid, slow changes get misread as self-excitation. Fix: M0 must include a slowly varying trend, so that any M1 gain is real and not spurious.
- **[Euromaidan Hawkes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.12253):** a discretized Hawkes model on counts. This supports our fallback, an hourly model with kernel sums.

**Assistant:**

Each change below has its possible downside and a short mitigation. Where I found none, I say so.

**From lbgos/AirAlerts:**
1. **Rings:** the risk is underfitting. Rings are symmetric, but attack routes have a direction; for example, region A may often be hit before B but not the other way round, and rings can't show that. Mitigation: compare the ring model against a model with directional pairs on validation.
2. **Recency weighting:** older data counts less, so there's less effective data, which makes parameter estimates noisier, especially for rare events and cross-region effects. It also forgets seasonal campaigns from a year ago (e.g. winter energy strikes), and the half-life is one more parameter to tune.
3. **Telegram alert channel:** it needs your credentials, so the organizers can't easily reproduce it. Message parsing errors could also create false alerts or lost endings, it may disagree with official data, and it costs time.
4. **"Confident but wrong" metric:** not a proper scoring rule, so choosing models by it pushes forecasts toward a timid 50%, and the 20%/80% cut-offs are arbitrary. Mitigation: use it only for reporting, never for choosing models.
5. **Live logging test:** it needs live data access and the code running for days, and a few days is a small, noisy sample. No harm to the model itself, only the time and setup it costs.

**From vladysalvkrutii/kse-air-alerts:**
6. **Automated leakage test:** no negative impact. Its only limit is that it can't catch leakage hidden in the source data itself (corrections made later).
7. **Pin the dataset, drop the last 24h:** this is in tension with "use the most recent data", because a pinned snapshot gets old and the freshest day is removed. Mitigation: re-pin to the latest commit right before the final run.
8. **Choose the training window on validation:** this overlaps with #2; two mechanisms tuning the same thing means more choices and more risk of overfitting the short validation period. A short window also leaves little data for cross-region effects. Mitigation: use one mechanism, or test both with a very small grid.

**From Ddrakkx/alerts-forecast:**
9. **Week-block bootstrap:** with only 4–8 test weeks the intervals are wide and themselves uncertain, so many differences will come out "not significant". That's honest, not harmful. No negative impact on the model.
10. **Per-region results:** no negative impact. Just remember that with 24 regions, a few will look good or bad by pure chance, so don't over-read single regions.

**From Dopplerr24/air-raid-alert-analysis:**
11. **Lag guard:** no negative impact.
12. **24h embargo:** it throws away the last day before each test window, which is the most informative data in a changing process. Our 24h-ahead labels already require a purge (no training label window may reach into the test period), and that purge is necessary. Mitigation: do the purge, skip the extra embargo.
13. **PR-AUC:** it depends on how often alerts happen, so it can't be compared across regions or periods with different rates, and it ignores calibration. Mitigation: report it, but choose models by log-likelihood and Brier. Dropping pooled ROC-AUC has no negative impact (we can still report it within each region to compare with other projects).

**From maranferij-lang/Ukraine-air-alerts:**
14. **Outage detection:** a real calm period could be mistaken for an outage and removed. That inflates the alert rate and deletes real information about lulls. Mitigation: mark a period as an outage only with independent evidence, e.g. all regions silent at once while another source shows alerts.
15. **Compare official vs volunteer files:** no negative impact, only time.
16. **Document negative experiments:** no negative impact.

**From koalla05/air-alerts:**
17. **Merge records into episodes:** the merging rule (how big a gap still counts as one alert) changes counts and durations. Merging oblast and raion records also loses the detail needed for hromada maps. Mitigation: keep both the raw and the merged versions, and check results under different gap rules.
18. **Kaplan-Meier baseline:** basically no negative impact. Its limitation: it assumes censoring is unrelated to duration, which may be false for alerts without an end message. That affects our main model too.
19. **Median + 10–90% range:** no negative impact on the model. The range may look very wide for long-tailed durations, but that's honest.

**From the IDS Hawkes paper:**
20. **Slowly varying trend in μ(t):** two real dangers.
    - **Leakage:** standard smoothing uses data on both sides of a point, including the future. The trend must be computed only from the past.
    - **Too flexible a trend absorbs real clustering:** the opposite error, hiding true self-excitation.
    Mitigation: a causal (past-only) trend, with its smoothness chosen on validation.

**From mykoladomanskyi25-dotcom:**
21. **7-day rolling mean baseline:** no negative impact.

**From Nujabesuuu/AlarmForecast:**
22. **Weather:** a serious leakage risk. At forecast time we know only the weather forecast, not the actual weather in the next hours, and archived historical forecasts are harder to get than observed weather. It's also another external data dependency, with a risk of chance correlations. Mitigation: use only weather known at time t (current observations or forecasts issued before t).

**From 3olena3:**
23. **Expected alert minutes in 24h:** no negative impact on the model. It just inherits errors from both models, so treat it as a rough figure.

**From tryvogy.com, air-alarms.in.ua and VoxUkraine:**
24. **Compare with external statistics:** their counting methods differ and have changed over time, so a mismatch may not mean we have a bug. That could waste time or give false reassurance. Mitigation: compare only roughly, as a sanity check.

**Risk across all changes:**
25. **More choices means more chances to fool ourselves.** Every tunable setting (half-life, window, trend smoothness, merge gap) is another way to overfit the validation period, a "garden of forking paths". Mitigation:
    - freeze the evaluation protocol before modeling;
    - keep the tuning grids small;
    - touch the test period only once.

## Summary

**No negative impact:** 6, 9, 10, 11, 15, 16, 18, 19, 21, 23.

**Accept with the mitigation:** 1, 2+8 (pick one mechanism), 4, 7, 12 (purge only), 13, 14, 17, 20, 22, 24.

**Accept, aware of the cost:** 3, 5.

**Assistant:**

By "one model" I mean one generative model with two linked parts: the start intensity λ (when alerts begin) and the survival function S (how long they last). Every output is produced by simulating it forward. The alternative is **separate direct models**, one per question or horizon (e.g. "start within 1h", "within 3h", "active at +5h"), which is what most other projects did.

## Pros of one generative model

1. **Consistent answers.** The chance of an alert within 3h can never be lower than within 1h, the map agrees with the "next alert" and "duration" panels, and duration quantiles are always in order.
2. **Interpretable.** Every number traces back to a few parameters (daily cycle, self-excitation, neighbor influence, duration distribution), and our hypotheses are tested as those parameters.
3. **Uses the data efficiently.** Each alert informs every horizon and every region at once; separate models split the data across many targets.
4. **Any question for free.** Any horizon (15 min, 7h, 24h), the expected total alert minutes, even **joint questions** like "chance that Kyiv and Lviv are both under alert at +3h". Separate models can't answer joint questions at all.
5. **Handles the on/off state correctly.** A region already under alert can't "start" one, and an unknown ending is treated as censored, not as a guess.
6. **One thing to validate.** A single goodness-of-fit test (time-rescaling) checks the whole structure.

## Cons of one generative model

1. **A wrong structure spoils everything at once.** If our assumptions are wrong (the Hawkes form, the decay shape, the duration distribution), every output is wrong in the same direction. A direct model tuned for one target is more robust to such mistakes.
2. **Errors build up over long horizons.** A 24h forecast is a chain of simulated steps, so small errors early in the chain grow. Direct models predict +20h in one step.
3. **Less flexible.** Gradient boosting can find complex interactions (e.g. "Sunday nights after a calm week") that a few-parameter formula won't capture.
4. **Slower.** Every forecast needs thousands of simulated scenarios for 23 regions, and the results carry a little simulation noise.
5. **Harder to build and debug.** Fitting a likelihood with many parameters can be unstable, and it needs careful mathematics and code.
6. **Hidden independence assumption.** If we assume durations don't depend on what's happening elsewhere, we may miss that during a mass attack alerts are both more frequent and longer. The duration model needs inputs about current national activity to avoid that.
7. **One point of failure.** If the model is bad, there's no alternative inside it.

## How our plan already reduces the cons

- **The ML challenger (D11)** is a direct model per horizon. It shows where the generative model loses (cons 1, 2 and 3) and acts as the backup (con 7).
- **The time-rescaling test and calibration checks** catch a wrong structure (con 1).
- **Duration inputs:** current national activity and time of day (con 6).

## Options

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| **a. Generative model only** | Fully consistent and interpretable | No backup if the structure is wrong |
| **b. Generative core + direct ML challenger, compared per horizon** (current D11) | Consistent core, honest check of weaknesses | More work |
| **c. Hybrid:** use whichever wins at each horizon | Best accuracy per horizon | Brings back inconsistency between views |

My suggestion: keep **b**, and decide about **c** only if the challenger clearly wins at some horizons. Then we'd see the size of the gain and judge whether it's worth the inconsistency.

Which option do you choose? The NOTES.md updates (Related work, changes 1–24, H7, the warnings, Known limitations, D13) are also still waiting for your OK.

## What changed after the research

**1. How we see the project.** Before, we didn't know if this was new. Now we know the topic is crowded: 12+ similar projects, at least 3 of them KSE applications for the same task, and two have a 24h map. A map or a high AUC alone won't stand out. What stands out is our mathematical core, since none of the projects I found used a point-process (Hawkes) model.

**2. Expectations about results.** Before, I had no reference point. Now: projects that measure carefully report **modest gains** (Brier skill +7%, within-region AUC 0.57–0.69, no gain for Poltava). Very high numbers (AUC 0.91) come from pooled metrics or unclear test setups. So our success criterion is an honest, measured gain over baselines, not a big number.

**3. Data.** Before, we had a list of candidate sources. Now we have specific warnings to verify in Step 4:
- the official file reportedly ends 2026-09-07;
- a feed outage on Aug 29 – Sep 3;
- official and volunteer files disagree;
- about 10% of alerts have no end message;
- Luhansk and Crimea have no usable data (D13).

**4. The model.** Before, we had a design. Now we have specific refinements:
- **rings** for cross-region influence, which make M2 practical (a few parameters instead of 625);
- **a past-only trend in μ(t)**, which protects H4 from a false result;
- outage masking;
- rules for censoring;
- Kaplan-Meier as the duration baseline.

**5. Evaluation.** Before, we had general rules. Now we have proven techniques:
- the leakage test with deliberately leaky features;
- the lag guard and the purge;
- bootstrap confidence intervals;
- per-region metrics;
- a wider baseline set;
- a prospective test.

**6. Risks.** Before, they were unclear. Now they're named: the cons of a single model, the Telegram problem, five unsolved limitations, and the danger of over-tuning.

## Did it actually help?

**Yes, in four specific ways:**
- **The data warnings.** Without them we might have built on a stale file and failed the "latest period" requirement without noticing.
- **The IDS paper warning.** Without it, we could have reported "strong self-excitation" that was really just a slowly changing alert rate. That would have been a mathematical error in our main claim.
- **The rings idea.** It turned M2 from impractical into feasible.
- **The leakage test pattern.** A concrete, checkable way to prove our main requirement.

**Where it didn't help, or has limits:**
- **We found no new data sources** beyond the ones we already knew, apart from the Telegram alert channel that lbgos used.
- **All the numbers are other people's claims.** Nothing is verified until we see our own output.
- **Nothing on hromada-level forecasting**, so that part is still uncertain.
- **It didn't change our core architecture; it confirmed it.** That's useful, but I read the projects with our plan in mind, which is a confirmation-bias risk. Also, "nobody tried Hawkes" doesn't prove it works; maybe it doesn't beat simpler models. Only our own test will show that.
- **It added complexity:** 24 changes means more work and more ways to over-tune. That's why the risk list matters.

Alert starts: point process with conditional intensity λ_r(t \| history before t), candidate form = multivariate Hawkes (seasonal baseline μ_r(t) via Fourier terms + self-excitation α_rr + cross-region excitation α_rs, decay kernel g; intensity active only in "off" state). Durations: survival analysis S(d) with censoring (log-normal / Weibull / mixture); remaining duration = S(e+x)/S(e). Map outputs (P(active at +h), next alert time, duration) all come from Monte Carlo simulation of the fitted model. Interface is minimal and only renders the model's probabilities | Pipeline/ML-centered plan with UI focus (rejected) | User: mathematical calculations must underpin every action; real impact and a model matter, not a beautiful interface |

74	## 5. Leakage checklist
75	- [ ] Censoring: an alert ongoing at time t has no known end time; never use its real end time as input.
76	- [ ] Rolling/lag features use only data strictly before t.
77	- [ ] Other regions' alerts are used only if they started before t.
78	- [ ] Timezones & DST handled consistently (Kyiv time vs UTC).
79	- [ ] Text data uses the original publication time, not edit or scrape time.
80	- [ ] Time-ordered split only: train on the past, test on the latest period. No random shuffling.
81	- [ ] Hyperparameters tuned on a validation period, never on the test period.

Known limitations (no full solution)\n1. Adversary decisions (start of a mass attack) cannot be predicted from alert history; Hawkes can only react once a wave starts.\n2. Freshness depends on dataset maintainers → backup source only reduces the risk.\n5. Predictability ceiling: careful projects all report modest gains; our goal is honest measurement, not impressive numbers.\n6. Separating self-excitation from a slowly changing rate is mathematically hard; only the out-of-sample test (M1 vs M0) decides.\n7. Telegram (Q13): unsolved until Step 4 facts are in."
}

===== datasets/README.md =====
## 🚨 About Datasets

There are two sources of alerts: official
and unofficial (collected by volunteers from [eTryvoga](https://app.etryvoga.com) channel).

Both datasets will be updated daily. All times are in UTC.

### Official dataset

You may see `official_data_en.csv` (🇬🇧) and `official_data_uk.csv` (🇺🇦) files.
They're identical but in different language.

Official dataset contains information from 15th of March 2022 – it's the first day when siren record occurs.
Since December, 2025th there is mostly air raid alerts on raion (district) level ([see post in the media](https://texty.org.ua/fragments/116501/v-ukrayini-zaprovadzhuyetsya-novyj-pidxid-do-oholoshennya-povitryanyx-tryvoh-svyrydenko/)), before sirens were applied to the whole oblast (region). You may find them on [wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raions_of_Ukraine).
On some .geojson files they're Subnational Administrative Boundaries (Admin 2: 139 Raion (District))

### Volunteer datasets

Data by volunteers are stored in `volunteer_data_uk.csv` (🇺🇦) and `volunteer_data_en.csv` (🇬🇧).

It contains more data (starts from 25th of February – second day of war!) and only on oblast (region) level.

If there are no messages about the end of the sirens,
you may see them with `naive=True` and `finished_at = started_at + 30 minutes`.

Thanks to [eTryvoga](https://app.etryvoga.com) channel for this data.

## 🤔 Good to Know

There are two permanent sirens:

1. In **Luhansk region** from April 4 at 04:45 PM (UTC+00) or April 4 at 07:45 PM (local time)
2. In **Crimea** from December 10 at 10:22 PM (UTC+00) or December 11 at 12:22 AM (local time)

They are not listed in datasets, so you may want to process them manually.

## Endpoints (base: `https://api.alerts.in.ua`)

- **Active alerts:** `/v1/alerts/active.json` returns regions with an active air raid or other threat, with details such as `alert_level`, `alert_type`, and `threats`.
- **Active status, all oblasts:** `/v1/iot/active_air_raid_alerts_by_oblast.json` returns a 27-character string, one status letter per oblast.
- **Active status, one region:** `/v1/iot/active_air_raid_alerts/{uid}.json` returns a single status for an oblast, raion, or city that declares alerts separately.
- **Active status, all regions:** `/v1/iot/active_air_raid_alerts.json` returns a string indexed by location UID.
- **History:** `/v1/regions/{uid}/alerts/{period}.json`. The only documented period is `month_ago`.

## History depth

The only documented period is `month_ago`, meaning one month before the current date. The doc does not describe anything older.

## Granularity

- Active alerts include `location_type` with values `oblast`, `raion`, `city`, `hromada`, or `unknown`, plus oblast and raion fields.
- The status endpoints cover oblasts, raions, and hromadas by UID.
- A full list of locations is linked as a Google Sheet. The doc only lists UIDs for oblasts and a few cities.

## Time format

Timestamps are ISO 8601 strings ending in `Z`, such as `2022-04-04T16:45:39.000Z`. The `Z` suffix conventionally means UTC, but the doc does not state the time zone explicitly.

## Authentication

- Access requires a personal API token. You request one through the form at `https://alerts.in.ua/api-request`.
- Pass the token as a query parameter (`?token=`) or as an `Authorization: Bearer` header.
- The doc says the token is a secret and that all activity under it is tied to your project.

## Rate limits and caching

- **Soft limit:** 8–10 requests per minute per IP.
- **Hard limit:** 12 requests per minute per IP.
- **History endpoint:** separate limit of 2 requests per minute.
- Exceeding limits returns HTTP 429. Systematic violations can get the IP and token blocked, and abnormal daily volume can get the token blocked.
- Caching: all APIs support `If-Modified-Since` with `Last-Modified`.
- The intro describes limits "per second," but the figures given are per minute.

## Usage restrictions

- **Public services:** the doc asks you to proxy requests through your own server and not to hardcode the token in client-side code. Physical devices that cannot use a proxy are exempt.
- **Critical infrastructure:** the doc says not to use the API for it.
- **Liability:** access and use are at your own discretion and risk. The service administration disclaims liability for direct or indirect damages. Updates may be delayed.
- **Agreement:** using the API means accepting the service's rules, which the doc refers to but does not include.
- **Research and redistribution:** the doc does not address these, so its terms do not answer them.
```

Ukraine is moving to a two-level air raid alert system, yellow and red, and the rollout is still underway, so the details vary by source.

- **Announcement:** Ukraine will update its air raid alert system and introduce two threat levels, yellow and red, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X on Sept. 2.
- **What each level means:** Zelenskyy's government says the yellow level indicates a drone attack, while the red level indicates a missile threat, ballistic missile threat, and massive attacks.
- **Who decides:** Ukraine's General Staff, Air Force, Cabinet of Ministers, Defense Ministry, Interior Ministry, and State Emergency Service will determine each week which threats correspond to yellow and red levels.
- **Siren changes:** The practice of sounding the siren a second time when the alert is lifted has been canceled, so the siren will now sound only while the alert is in effect. Ukraine will also change the warning signals so they match the yellow or red threat level.
- **Start date conflict:** One report says Ukrainian authorities in Kyiv implemented the new air raid alert system on September 6. Lviv is a separate case: the relevant changes will take effect from October 12. Lviv's all-clear will also be voiced by a female voice, and the siren sound will no longer be used.
- **Possible error in one result:** A 112.ua item says Ukraine has used a differentiated air raid alert system with yellow and red levels since September 2023. That conflicts with the 2026 announcement and may be a dating error, so I would not rely on it without checking.

Overall, the national framework was announced on September 2, Kyiv reportedly began using it on September 6, and other cities such as Lviv are adopting it on their own timelines. For an official schedule, check the Ukrainian government or your city council.

**Постанова КМУ № 1092 від 4 вересня 2026 року** розділила повітряні тривоги на два рівні: жовтий і червоний.

**Що означає кожен рівень**
- **Жовтий** стосується загрози від дронів. Один із джерел описує його як сигнал про присутність безпілотників, коли ситуація ще не набула масованого характеру (Він сигналізує про загрозу нижчої інтенсивності, коли фіксується присутність безпілотників, але ситуація ще не набула масованого характеру.).
- **Червоний** охоплює ракетну, ракетно-дронову або масовану дронову загрозу (червоний рівень – ракетна, ракетно-дронова або масована дронова загроза).
- Тривалість сигналу відрізняється: за жовтого рівня він звучить 30 секунд, за червоного – 1 хвилину (сигнал тривоги має тривати 30 секунд для жовтого рівня та 1 хвилину для червоного).

**Правила для бізнесу та закладів**
- Під час жовтого рівня бізнес може працювати. Якщо укриття немає, це можливо за погодженням із трудовим колективом, і лише тимчасово, не довше трьох місяців від набрання чинності постановою (Підприємство, де немає тимчасового або постійного укриття, може продовжувати діяльність під час жовтого рівня за погодженням із трудовим колективом. Але лише тимчасово до облаштування укриття і не довше трьох місяців із дня набрання чинності Постановою №1092.).
- Заклади освіти не отримали послаблень: за обох рівнів учні, вихованці та працівники переходять в укриття (Якщо оголошено повітряну тривогу, учні й працівники школи мають перейти в укриття — незалежно від того, жовтий це чи червоний рівень.).

**Що сталося у вересні 2026**
- Перехід на нову систему відбувався поетапно. Один із джерел вказує, що диференціація діяла з 8 вересня, а в деяких регіонах раніше (починаючи з 08.09.2026 (а в деяких регіонах — раніше), в Україні запроваджено диференціацію тривог за рівнем загрози). Для Києва інше джерело називає 6 вересня (З 6:00 години 6 вересня 2026 року в Києві запроваджується диференційоване оповіщення про повітряні загрози). Дати різняться, тому для точних даних варто звернутися до офіційних джерел.
- За підсумками місяця частка жовтих тривог становила 60,9 %, червоних – 39,1 % від усіх ідентифікованих тривог (за даними УРТЦ, тривоги жовтого рівня протягом вересня становили 60,9 % від тривалості всіх ідентифікованих тривог, а червоного — 39,1 %).
- 29 вересня червоний рівень оголошували в Києві та низці областей через загрозу балістики (У Києві та низці областей був оголошений червоний рівень повітряної тривоги через загрозу застосування росіянами балістики.).

**Зміни від 15 вересня:** постанова № 1092 була доповнена постановою № 1128 від 15.09.2026, яка уточнила вимоги до сигналу, приміщень і дій бізнесу (постанова КМУ №1128 уточнила вимоги до сигналу, приміщень і дій бізнесу).

Більшість джерел – юридичні та бізнес-портали, тому для роботодавців варто перевіряти текст самої постанови на офіційному сайті Кабміну або в Офіційному віснику.
